title: Classical gold standard
summary: Under the gold standard a country fixed the price of its currency in gold and let notes and deposits be freely converted. Britain, on gold since 1821, was the centre; Germany adopted it in 1871, and France and the United States followed in 1878-79, with most countries by 1880. The Bank of England kept the system working by raising its rate when gold ran out. The era brought price stability and fast growth with free movement of goods, labour and capital, and it broke down when war came in 1914.

uncertainty.note: Germany established its gold coin standard in 1871, sparking widespread adoption across Europe and North America through the 1870s, lasting until general suspension at the outbreak of World War I in 1914.

as_recorded.value: The period from 1880 to 1914 is known as the classical gold standard

where.modern_name: Bank of England, London, United Kingdom (financial hub of the international gold standard)
where.historical_name: Bank of England, London, British Empire

importance.justification: The monetary order of the first global economy, tying world prices, trade and capital flows together (R4 D2 T2 L3).

related.because: Econlib: the gold standard broke down in the First World War as belligerents resorted to inflationary finance.
